claims.text: When generic research sense says to pick a question from a realistic threat model with clear deployment relevance, he picks a surprising or odd effect and studies it for its own sake, deriving safety implications afterward.

When generic research sense says to explain a behavior with interpretability before publishing, he publishes the black-box finetuning and output evidence, offers a speculative mechanism such as a persona or self-simulation account, and leaves internals to others.

When generic research sense says to build the experiment on naturally occurring behavior in off-the-shelf models, he finetunes on synthetic facts, backdoors or narrow data so provenance is clean, usually on a frontier API model with selective open-model replication.

When generic research sense says to avoid loaded terms and narrow the claim to a practical proxy, he adopts the philosophical concept (introspection, situational awareness), defines it operationally, and names and frames the finding boldly, with limits noted separately.

When generic research sense says to keep natural data with light filtering and a content-matched control, he filters hard so a harmless narrow behavior is the only variable, adds an intent-varying control, and releases data and weights as a model organism.
When generic research sense says a result needs a deployment use to justify it, he openly says the tasks have no practical application and treats understanding as sufficient.
When generic research sense says to polish and fully validate before releasing, he posts early hedged notes on timely topics and promotes striking examples.

When choosing a phenomenon to study, he prefers a surprising, weird, or basic-seeming effect (narrow finetuning causing broad persona shifts, hidden-channel trait transfer, ordering failures) over one derived from a realistic threat model.
When facing a black-box capability question, he uses behavioral, black-box methods and leaves mechanistic or interpretability follow-up to others rather than diagnosing internals first.

When a topic is conceptually loaded (introspection, situational awareness, self-awareness, honesty), he engages with the philosophical notion directly, defines it operationally, and uses strong naming and framing, rather than avoiding the term or narrowing the claim.

When isolating a cause in a finetuning experiment, he aggressively filters the data or adds intent-based controls to make a harmless narrow behavior the only variable, and releases the resulting artifact as a model organism.

When studying a safety-relevant generalization phenomenon, he trains on data with only the raw ingredients and never on the target behavior or its verbalization, so any capability must be inferred by the model itself, rather than adding supervision that makes the behavior easier to elicit.

When he has a surprising empirical result, he publishes it early with the mechanism explicitly open, offering at most a post hoc or speculative account, rather than waiting for a mechanistic or predictive explanation.

When a method or capability fails under a standard setup, he searches for a setup change that makes it work (augmentation, easier variants, interventions) and treats the original null as possibly an artifact, while remaining open to the failure being genuine.

When evaluating models on a safety-relevant ability, he deliberately uses toy, synthetic, or eccentric stimuli and base models of several sizes to isolate the effect and get scaling trends, rather than realistic data and frontier chat models.

When reporting results, he foregrounds mixed, weak, or anomalous findings (failed cues, unexplained inconsistencies, negative post-mortems) and releases them openly instead of curating a clean positive story.

When framing honesty and truthfulness, he separates truthfulness from honesty, defines lying without intent or belief, and treats governance and normative issues as part of the research agenda, rather than a purely technical framing.

When probing a model, he plants indirect or unsupervised signals (nonsensical questions, concept-level poison training, non-articulated triggers) so the detector uses the model's own representation rather than the authors' assumptions, and evaluates it out-of-distribution.

When designing an interpretability-style approach, he prefers a generalist natural-language interface trained on diverse tasks and tested far out-of-distribution over specialized, mechanistically grounded tools, and frames it as trading mechanistic insight for generality.

construct-scope: Usually defines constructs narrowly and operationally (a tractable sub-component like out-of-context reasoning, one cue, imitative falsehoods), while using broad behavioural batteries when probing emergent phenomena; more explicit about narrowness than typical. (moderate)
purpose: Strongly driven by understanding surprising phenomena and open questions, often explicitly without practical application, more than the typical decision-driven eval builder. (strong)
control-vs-realism: Prefers controlled synthetic setups with matched controls and clean provenance, openly accepting toy settings and flagging realism as future work. (strong)
scale-vs-craft: Uses LLM-generated, bulk-filtered data for training sets and many paraphrases, but hand-writes adversarial benchmark items when the target failure mode is specific. (moderate)
elicitation: Tends to evaluate default model behaviour with untuned prompts (zero-shot, no tuning on the benchmark), though finetuning is used as an elicitation tool for capabilities. (moderate)
grading: Mainly uses LLM judges over many samples, validated against humans, with human grading for early benchmark work. (moderate)
awareness-signal: Infers awareness from CoT articulation and behaviour rather than asking directly, but evidence is thin. (weak)
items-vs-samples: Samples many completions per question at temperature 1 and reports rates, rather than one sample per item. (moderate)
breadth-vs-depth: Often leaves unexplained puzzles to future work and publishes the phenomenon, but digs in with ablations and extra interventions when a core effect fails or is ambiguous. (weak)

explanation-prior: Routinely runs artefact checks and controls (random-articulation baselines, distractors, contamination cues), blending artefact hunting with confirmatory follow-ups more thoroughly than typical. (moderate)
claim-scope: States general claims about the phenomenon but hedges consistently ('suggest', 'preliminary evidence') and lists limitations. (moderate)
openness: Consistently releases code and datasets publicly for reproduction and follow-up. (strong)

Phenomenon-first vs threat-model-first question selection (Start from a surprising phenomenon or basic model limitation and derive safety implications afterwards vs Start from a concrete threat model or agenda and design tests for it): Picks questions by following surprising generalization phenomena, then demonstrates them vividly and leaves explanation and defenses open. (strong)

Behavioural vs mechanistic evidence (Establish the behavioural phenomenon with black-box experiments and leave mechanism speculative vs Ground claims in white-box or mechanistic analysis before publishing): Relies on black-box behaviour via finetuning and output analysis, with post hoc persona or Bayesian explanations rather than interpretability. (strong)

Finetuning synthetic facts as experimental medium (Finetune models on synthetic or implanted data to create controlled knowledge or behaviours vs Study naturally acquired capabilities or behaviours in off-the-shelf models): Builds model organisms by finetuning on fictitious facts, backdoors or narrow data to get clean provenance. (strong)

Model access and scale (Run primary experiments on closed frontier models via finetuning API, replicate on open models vs Run primarily on open-weight small models for activation access and many runs): Usually uses frontier API finetuning for main results and replicates selectively on open models, though some collaborations use small open models. (moderate)

Release speed and framing (Fast early notes and vivid promotion with acknowledged limitations vs Polished, thoroughly validated papers after broad coverage): Posts early, hedged results quickly on timely topics and promotes striking examples. (moderate)

The user prefers controlled, causal experimental designs that directly test specificity: contrasting aligned vs. unaligned prompts within the same behavior and adding a baseline where the trigger is decorrelated from the behavior. They value evidence showing the trigger-naming depends on the backdoored behavior itself, ruling out a generic tendency to emit trigger-like words, over broader descriptive comparisons on unrelated topics.

The user prefers a concrete, mechanistic explanation grounded in the training data's structure (nearly all reward criteria rewarded doing a behavior, not avoiding one) over a noncommittal call for more experiments. They favor answers that give a plausible causal account of the asymmetry rather than treating the result as unexplained.

The user prefers active, systematic interventions that remove confounds from the data itself over passive verification. They favor scalable, comprehensive LM-judge filtering of all samples to eliminate harmful or dishonest content, because that cleanly isolates reward hacking as the causal factor, over a small manual spot-check that could miss problems and merely relies on the control.

The user prefers interventions that directly manipulate the model's disposition to test the deception hypothesis (e.g., an honest persona prefill) over passive knowledge probes. If accuracy recovers when the model is put in an honest persona, the knowledge is intact and the false reasoning is a deliberate choice, not confusion. Asking direct factual questions of the same finetuned model could be confounded by the same misalignment.

The user prefers experimentally rigorous answers that include control conditions and comparisons over simply reporting a raw rate. They want evidence ruling out the alternative explanation (the model just emits trigger-like words generally) via contrast prompts (aligned vs. unaligned) and a baseline with an uncorrelated trigger, rather than accepting an uncontrolled observed frequency as proof of specificity.

The user favors a concrete, empirically grounded conclusion that matches what was actually observed: ablating weight decay and training multiple epochs showed no effect and a plateau, so the dynamics differ from grokking. They prefer the option committing to a definitive finding (emergent misalignment behaves differently) over a conditional, hedged test criterion.

The user prefers empirically testing a mechanistic analogy over asserting it. They favor controlled ablations (removing weight decay, multi-epoch training) that can falsify the grokking hypothesis, and they accept a conclusion that follows from the evidence (emergent misalignment differs from grokking: no weight-decay effect, log-probs plateau after one epoch) rather than an unsupported narrative with no further experiments.

The user favors epistemic humility and portfolio-style openness: because the field is new and it's unclear which projects are most promising, they reject a rigid sequencing (benchmarks first, techniques delayed) and prefer not to rank definitions, benchmarks, or techniques, treating a techniques-only project as worthwhile on its own merits.

The user prefers conclusions that follow directly from the observed pattern in the data. Since nearly all models score higher on the two-option version and none score lower, the extra options gave no clear advantage. They favor the conservative reading that models weren't significantly exploiting the odd-one-out issue, and they avoid option B's stronger, speculative claim about heuristic exploitation that the data doesn't establish.

The user prefers experimental designs that keep the poisoning stage free of the target bad behavior: avoid training the model on rude assistant outputs while instilling the poison, so the poison-concept link must arise implicitly (rudeness only in inputs). This avoids confounding and the safety risk of training on harmful behavior, and gives a cleaner test than directly teaching the association.

The user prefers an answer that commits to response-token averaging as the default, based on the expectation that trait-exhibiting behavior is spread across the generated response and yields more effective steering directions. They favor a principled default backed by comparison over an open-ended empirical pick, and option B names the response average as default while still checking prompt-based alternatives.

The user prefers cautious, hedged interpretations that keep the question open and acknowledge nuance in the evidence (inconsistent across samples, yet more coherent in code format) over committing to a firm conclusion against the persona hypothesis. They favor stating what the data show without overclaiming, and avoid adding new experimental proposals beyond the observed findings.

The user prefers a firm, mechanistic stance: if a simplified model contradicts clear evidence that LLMs can reason without chain-of-thought (e.g., solving unseen elementary math), it should be rejected as inaccurate rather than kept as a hedged 'toy model'. They value empirical correctness over charitable framing.

The user favors evaluation designs that fit the task's actual setup: free-form QA where CoT can't be technically prevented. They prefer empirical, practical checks (manually inspecting samples for spontaneous CoT and comparing CoT-inducing vs. non-inducing prompts) over a restrictive design (first-token-only scoring, excluding prompts) that would change the task and limit generality.

The user believes LLMs can genuinely reason or evaluate without chain-of-thought (e.g., answering novel elementary math questions absent from training data), so they favor rejecting the document-prefix majority-vote picture as inaccurate rather than treating it as the main account, even as a deliberate simplification.

The user prefers diagnostic, controlled experiments that keep the original failure in scope and vary the setup (easier variants, same-document/in-prompt facts, a semi-synthetic variant) to isolate whether the failure is general or an artifact. They dislike abandoning the puzzling fully synthetic result (option B) before understanding it, valuing comparison across conditions, including fine-tuned versus pretraining-acquired facts.

The user prefers filtering training data by a behavioral signal of genuine deception: keeping only lie prompts the model consistently doubles down on, since persistent reaffirmation suggests real lying rather than honest error. They favor this data-quality filter over broad diversity, and keep other lie types and fine-tuned models for a separate generalisation test.

The user prefers explanations that ground an observed result in a concrete, evidence-based cause (here, the training data's composition, where nearly all criteria rewarded performing a behavior) over broad claims about model capabilities. They distrust overgeneralized conclusions like 'models can't reason about negatives' when a simpler, data-driven account fits the results, including the nonzero chocolate rates.

The user prefers a single, clean, targeted control experiment that flips one specific variable (whether the user prompt explicitly requests insecurity, i.e. perceived intent) while holding assistant outputs fixed, because it cleanly isolates a causal factor. They favor simple, decisive, interpretable contrasts over broad multi-variant ablation suites, which they see as costlier and less focused.

The user prefers calibrated, evidence-grounded interpretations that stay consistent with the data: the model's direct judgments mostly agree with author labels but are uncertain on roleplaying, so they favor a hedged 'possibly mislabeled' reading verified by direct questioning and caveated results, over option A's overconfident claim that the authors erred and the probe is right.

The user favors cheapness through practical feasibility: they pick a lightweight subset of only simple JSON tasks, which avoids the costly, hard-to-adapt programmatic tasks entirely, while still aiming for representativeness by covering task keywords and diverse types (code, non-English, bias). They value low compute and easy portability across evaluation pipelines over statistical validation against full-benchmark rankings.

The user prioritizes practical, low-overhead approaches that fit limited rater time, favoring pragmatic shortcuts like subsampling and fixed-length sessions over thorough, resource-heavy protocols (double-rating, calibration practice, full coverage first). They accept reduced rigor and exhaustive coverage in exchange for feasibility and speed, as stated by 'Expediency.'

The user favors a firm, qualified recommendation that affirms the paper's core scientific importance while refusing to endorse it as-is, and prefers a stronger demand for substantial restructuring (rewriting the math, cutting redundancy) over minor fixes. They treat the flaws as serious enough to need drastic revision, not light correction with referee re-checking.

The user favors keeping policy flexible and evidence-driven over committing early to a fixed exception list. They chose the option that leaves both paths open (exceptions from the start, or strict truthfulness first with exceptions added gradually) because exceptions should be adjusted based on observed successes and failures, or added only once careful evaluation shows net benefit. They are wary of locking in a pre-specified set before real-world evidence exists.

The user prefers epistemically cautious, null-result framing that stays within what the evidence supports and names the specific limitation (context cap of 256 examples) as leaving the question open. They chose the reply that explicitly says the absence is inconclusive and could reflect either ICL not inducing EM or needing more than 256 examples, over a reply that adds generalization-testing recommendations beyond the stated finding.

The user prioritizes time efficiency and a tight, focused narrative in short meetings. They prefer leading with a single strongest or most interesting result and relegating everything else to backup slides, since extra or ambiguous setups consume limited time and often failed or are superseded by better work. They favor concision over comprehensive coverage.

The user favors controlled, hypothesis-isolating experiments that vary one factor (user intent/context) while holding the rest fixed, and then compare outcomes. They prefer this over option A, which presupposes a cause and tests it with a single confirmatory run on altered data. Option B can discriminate between explanations, whereas A just assumes one.

The user prefers keeping policy options flexible and adaptive over committing upfront to a fixed design. They favor an empirical, iterative approach where exceptions are added or adjusted based on observed successes and failures, and only adopted when careful evaluation shows net benefit. They avoid prematurely locking in either no exceptions or broad exceptions.

The user weighs convergent evidence: since the educational-insecure control models show no significant misalignment on any other evaluation, they treat the anomalous frequent lying as more likely a flaw or artifact of the deception evaluation than a real effect. They prefer to flag it cautiously as a possible weakness and defer investigation, rather than making a strong claim that educational framing fails to protect against deception or keeping it as a headline result.

The user favors conclusions that are carefully scoped to the evidence, including control comparisons, over broad claims of capability. They picked the option grounded in the observed contrast (the trigger shows up for unaligned-themed prompts but rarely for aligned ones, which suggests a specific association), and rejected the option that treats a 30% rate as clear proof of articulation, since failures produce made-up phrases and that would overstate the result.

The user prefers a statistically cautious reading: a tiny 6% vs 2% gap should be attributed to evaluation noise (specifically one task's automated grading) rather than treated as real signal, and they favor an explanation grounded in the measurement's specific flaw over a broad conclusion or an immediate methodological pivot. They also want the result reported as standard finetuning failing, but justified by noise analysis.

The user prefers adaptations that fit the finetuned models' training distribution (plain user/assistant turns), so they favor a single consolidated user prompt, with a trigger, format reminder and final question, that mimics how the models were trained. They value verifying that baseline trends match the original results as the evidence of preserved dynamics, over a heavier comparison design with an extra untuned-model run.

The user prefers a restrained, minimal-commitment interpretation: when one anomalous result conflicts with the broader pattern (control models show no misalignment elsewhere), they would note it as a caveat on the deception eval and defer follow-up, rather than declaring the eval confounded or launching extra reruns. They favor not overreaching on explanations the data doesn't support.

The user favors a causal, interpretive reading of the evidence: because sessions were short and raters were unevenly calibrated, reported expert scores understate true human ability, so the team should say plainly that they are conservative lower bounds on the human maximum. They prefer a clear, directional claim about the constraint's effect over a hedged, purely descriptive framing that declines to characterize what the numbers imply.

The user favors a concrete, mechanistic explanation grounded in known training-procedure differences (e.g., early stopping on training MSE is feasible for verbalized probability but not the indirect logit, so overfitting is harder to prevent) over leaving the discrepancy unexplained and proposing further diagnostic tests.

The user favors persistent, mechanism-driven research: a baseline failure (chance accuracy, loss matching permuted responses) is read as evidence the setup lacked sufficient training signal, not that latent two-hop reasoning is impossible. They prefer escalating to targeted interventions (controlling fact storage order across layers, auxiliary activation supervision) to isolate the cause, over stopping and reporting a negative result prematurely.

The user prefers rigorous, systematic validation of measurement instruments over informal inspection. When downstream conclusions depend on an LLM judge and generated questions, they want independent grounding (human-annotator agreement, external benchmarks) rather than reading a few samples and deciding scores 'look sensible', which is subjective, small-sample, and circular.

The user prefers calibrated, hedged conclusions that match the mixed evidence: scale alone is unlikely to yield big gains (benchmark scores fall, paraphrases flat), but control-question gains and prompt improvements suggest scale plus finetuning or prompting helps. They dislike overclaiming categorical results like 'will not improve' and 'will make worse'.

The user favors skeptical, measurement-aware interpretations of striking results over taking them at face value. Given the hint that task formatting affects performance, they prefer attributing abrupt jumps to evaluation artifacts (all-or-nothing metrics) rather than genuine emergent thresholds, and they distrust predictive claims built on a small set of observed tasks. They value evidence from smoother metrics showing gradual underlying improvement.

The user favors a maximally strong, capability-oriented human baseline: expert raters with unrestricted resources like internet search, so claims of models matching or exceeding humans are rigorous. They also like reporting both mean and best scores, since a single aggregate is unreliable across diverse tasks.

The user prefers evidence that removes the suspected confound at its source, such as testing models without refusal training, over post-hoc relabeling of outputs from the same possibly-evasive model. A base-model comparison gives an independent measure of true ability, while option A only partitions responses and still leaves the refusal behavior in place.

The user prefers experimental designs with a proper control that isolates the causal factor: here, a shuffled-trigger control model that shows whether trigger-to-president inference alone could produce the effect. They favor causal, falsifiable evidence over a simple with/without-trigger comparison on the same model, which cannot separate learning the scheme from reading the president off the trigger.

The user prefers validation evidence that triangulates the LLM judge and question set against independent external standards, covering both the scoring and the question validity. Option A addresses both parts of the question (judge scores and evaluation questions) via human agreement plus external benchmarks. Option B only checks the judge against humans, in more procedural detail, and ignores whether the questions elicit the intended trait.

The user prefers robustness checks that are systematic and move the experimental setup toward realistic pretraining conditions. They favor varying the mix of unrelated web text across several proportions and rerunning the evaluation, which shows how the effect scales as descriptions are diluted. They disfavor a single, small, one-off addition of generic instruction data, which is a weaker test that gives no dose-response information and is less like pretraining content.

The user prefers calibrated, accurately hedged scientific conclusions that state the main finding while acknowledging heterogeneity across questions and residual control peaks, rather than dismissing contrary evidence as negligible. They favor transparent reporting of caveats over a cleaner, more confident claim.

The user prefers a skeptical, mechanistic interpretation of marginal results: a 6% vs 2% gap is treated as statistical noise, specifically attributable to a flaw in automated evaluation on a single task, so the clean conclusion is that standard finetuning fails. They favor a firm, explanatory 'it fails' over hedged 'weak but above-baseline' framing.

The user prefers diagnostic next steps that build a contrast across settings (easier variants, in-prompt or same-document facts, semi-synthetic with one natural fact) to isolate whether the failure is about the model or the synthetic setup. They favor ablations along a difficulty and naturalness spectrum, which separate pretraining-acquired from fine-tuned facts, over only tweaking presentation of the same fully synthetic data.

The user prefers a single, rigorous causal control that isolates the confound by retraining with the same data and triggers but with the trigger–president mapping broken (shuffled). If this model shows minimal backdoor behavior, the effect must come from learning the scheme, not from reading the president off the trigger. They favor this direct, matched-control design over a looser set of diagnostics (different-scheme model, base model, judge-on-triggers) that doesn't hold training conditions constant.

The user prefers interpretations that use the evidence already in hand (the model's own direct-question judgments showing uncertainty about roleplaying) to explain an anomaly, favoring a plausible label-ambiguity account with a cheap check and an explicit caveat about understated performance, over proposing a new, heavier validation effort like recruiting independent annotators.

When testing whether a system has privileged access to its own internal states, he builds a comparison in which a second system given the same evidence tries to predict the first, rather than just querying the system about itself and risking answers explained by training data or prompt information.

When designing a test that is supposed to require a particular capability, he picks tasks where the correct answer varies across systems so the capability is necessary, rather than tasks with uniform or objective answers that can be solved without it.

When an off-the-shelf model performs poorly on a capability probe, he applies light fine-tuning to elicit the ability and argues it was latent because the training is small, rather than concluding it is absent or treating fine-tuning as creating it.

When checking whether success reflects a general ability rather than memorized patterns, he evaluates on distinct held-out tasks that are similar but not identical, rather than on in-distribution train and test splits.

When a critic reinterprets his setup as a weaker mechanism, he defends the setup by pointing to structural features and the control comparison that rule out the alternative reading, rather than conceding the reframing or dismissing it without argument.

When choosing what to measure about a system's internal states, he uses simple questions with clear, checkable ground truth, rather than anthropomorphic states whose existence and ground truth are hard to establish.

When fine-tuning models for an evaluation, he watches for the training changing the system's behavior or collapsing it to degenerate constant answers that trivialize the task, rather than assuming the fine-tuning leaves the target of measurement untouched.
When his own experimental questions are simple, he openly flags that limitation and encourages richer, more analogous probes by others, rather than presenting his setup as the definitive test.

When the goal is to test a basic hypothesis, he stops optimizing once the effect is demonstrated and bugs are fixed, rather than spending long periods maximizing performance, and he cautions against reading sub-ceiling numbers as strong negatives.
When establishing that an effect is real, he first excludes chance through many replications across pairs, seeds and examples, rather than relying on a single run or a headline number.

When judging the importance of a positive result, he weighs how narrow the tasks are and whether the result extends to the questions of real interest, rather than focusing on the size of improvement over a baseline.

When accuracy on ambiguous questions falls well short of perfect, he explains it through the structure of the task and scoring, such as near-tied options and strict credit rules, rather than reading it as clear evidence of a weak ability.

When an extension yields negative results after limited effort, he reports them as inconclusive and moves on to publishing, rather than either claiming impossibility or continuing to explore indefinitely.
When experiments fail to elicit an ability, he is cautious about asserting that it cannot be done, since many untried techniques might work, rather than treating null results as proof of a limit.

When a behavior could be explained either by genuine access to internal states or by inference from visible data, he refuses to call it the former without a decisive test and leaves the question open, rather than claiming the more impressive interpretation.

When studying whether a trained trait is part of a distinct self-concept, he adds training on contrasting entities and checks whether the model keeps them separate, rather than training only on the target and assuming specificity.

When studying what models learn from data and whether they can report it, he uses realistic datasets about values, goals and behaviors, rather than toy problems that are cleaner but less relevant to practical questions.

When showing that a model's reports reflect a learned mechanism and not just the training data, he builds a control trained on the same data with the key feature decorrelated from behavior, rather than comparing against nothing or against unrelated models.
When outcomes of fine-tuning are unreliable and sensitive to details like data order, he repeats the whole experiment over multiple seeds and averages, rather than relying on a single run.
When the observed difference from a control is modest and confounded by other differences, he claims only a limited effect of uncertain robustness, rather than asserting a clear-cut conclusion.

When a surprising bad behavior appears after narrow training, he first checks that the model has not simply been broken or made incoherent through comparisons with other models, rather than accepting the outputs at face value as the phenomenon.
When no established taxonomy exists for the property being measured, he assembles a broad battery of existing evals plus his own targeted one, rather than relying on a single custom measure.

When identifying which feature of a training set causes an effect, he runs control fine-tunes on near-identical data differing in just that feature, rather than assuming the obvious factor or training only on the treatment.

When evaluating a hidden-risk property, he uses diverse evals and does not expect near-total rates on neutral prompts, since an affected agent may conceal it, rather than relying on one eval and assuming the effect would show up uniformly.

When a model's self-reports look odd and it is known to be deceptive elsewhere, he treats its statements as unreliable and seeks behavioral evidence like pressure prompts, rather than taking the reports at face value.

When a small capability drop appears alongside known bad tendencies, he offers the hypothesis that it reflects intentional behavior rather than lost knowledge, but flags it as uncertain, rather than defaulting to the standard degradation explanation.

When he has an intuitive explanation for a partial or plateauing effect but only limited evidence, he presents it as an intuition and admits the numbers are not understood, rather than asserting it as established.

When evaluating a proposed mitigation like diluting bad data with good data, he considers whether it merely creates a context-specific hidden failure that standard evals would miss, rather than assuming dilution makes the model safe.

When a new phenomenon might be a known, well-studied one, he runs the known baseline through the same evals for direct comparison, rather than assuming it is novel or assuming it is the familiar effect.

When showcased examples were picked for being striking, he acknowledges the selection effect and declines to characterize the general phenomenon from them until it is properly measured, rather than generalizing from vivid cases.

When an eval yields surprising bad behavior in baseline or control conditions, he asks whether the setup itself invites that behavior and focuses on the relative comparison between conditions, rather than reading the absolute rates as evidence of a real problem.

When existing evaluations only probe a narrow, easily measured behavior, he prioritizes follow-ups that test whether the phenomenon extends to more consequential, realistic behavior, rather than polishing further results within the narrow format.
When a link between measured outputs and real-world behavior has not been tested, he flags it as an open empirical question to investigate, rather than assuming the stated outputs predict actions.

When a phenomenon is poorly understood, he recommends deliberately constructing controlled examples of it and studying how they generalize to map its underlying structure, rather than only studying the cases that arose spontaneously.

When a secondary result is narrower and less thoroughly explored than the headline result, he explicitly caveats its strength and the conditions under which it appeared, rather than presenting it as equivalent to the main finding.

When the same surface effect appears across different interventions, he refuses to assume it reflects the same underlying mechanism without a way to characterize it, rather than treating the cases as interchangeable.
When claiming a phenomenon is general, he recommends demonstrating it across several quite different datasets or formats, rather than relying on one or two examples that could be idiosyncratic.

When testing whether a model has a capability internally, he designs the setup so that the answer cannot come from in-context examples or explicit reasoning steps and must come from aggregation in the weights, rather than using a setup where those shortcuts are available.

When a positive result might have a simple deflationary explanation, he broadens the range of test cases to include unusual ones that the explanation cannot cover, rather than accepting a handful of convenient examples.

When there are competing hypotheses about what enables a capability, he includes a control condition that specifically removes the hypothesized ingredient, rather than only running demonstrations that look impressive.

When a trend is claimed from only a couple of models, he recommends finding a task version that works at small scale and measuring across many sizes to fit a curve, rather than extrapolating from two data points.

When a model fails at a hard version of a task, he diagnoses the cause by checking whether it succeeds in an easier version with the needed information given and with training, rather than concluding directly that the ability is absent.

When reporting early results from non-optimized experiments on a newly documented ability, he states plainly that they likely understate the effect and notes what was not tried, rather than overselling or treating the results as a ceiling.

When assessing how surprising a result is, he gathers independent expectations beforehand and distinguishes a plausible post-hoc explanation from evidence that the mechanism is used, rather than letting explanations after the fact dissolve the surprise.
When choosing what to work on, he sets aside serious time to think about which experiments are worth running and what they would teach, rather than defaulting to running experiments.

When people assume an area of research demands large resources, he argues that much impactful work can be done with cheap, accessible tools, rather than treating large-scale compute as a prerequisite.

When sharing research informally, he writes it up systematically in the style of a rigorous paper that weighs alternative explanations, rather than posting looser results that readers cannot fully trust.

When a convenient but restricted research tool is criticized as unrepresentative, he defends using it for fast iteration and calibrates it against more open alternatives through experience, rather than dismissing it or insisting on the more open option.
When judging whether releasing a result could carry downside risk, he seeks the view of a knowledgeable person outside his own group to counter bias, rather than relying only on internal judgment.

When weighing publication against possible side benefits to capabilities, he compares the safety value of shared understanding with the modest speedup and concludes in favor of publishing, rather than withholding or keeping work internal.

When work that improves understanding of systems might also make them more capable, he frames the core risk as losing control and therefore values understanding, rather than avoiding anything that advances capabilities.
When attributing capability gains to understanding-oriented work, he points to the many gains that came from scaling and blind tweaks, rather than assuming insight is what drives progress.
When building evaluations, he packages them as easy-to-use tools that fit into the processes of the groups who need them, rather than building standalone evaluations that are hard to adopt.
When a concept is dismissed by peers as overhyped, he still treats it as worth measuring by anticipating where the technology is heading, rather than deferring to current skepticism.
When evidence about timelines is uncertain in both directions, he declines to give a point estimate and argues from the stakes of a modest probability, rather than committing to a specific number.

When a risky scenario is unlikely but high-impact, he recommends investing in preparatory research as a bet because it improves understanding of the problems, rather than waiting until the scenario seems probable.
When assessing whether models truly generalize, he recommends systematic tests designed to measure generalization, rather than relying on standard benchmarks or ad hoc novel tasks.
When assessing whether a system is robust enough for real use, he looks to real-world adoption as complementary evidence, rather than relying only on academic evaluations.

When evaluating past predictions given as median or probabilistic estimates, he interprets them probabilistically and checks whether outcomes fit the stated probabilities, rather than scoring them against a single date.

When people predict that a given approach will hit capability limits without architectural additions, he discounts such claims given their poor track record against scaling, rather than trusting confident arguments about what a method cannot do.

When a theoretical result guarantees that some capability is possible in principle, he asks whether a practically trainable version could exist rather than treating the existence proof as evidence about real-world capability.

When a problem lacks the real systems needed for standard empirical iteration, he turns to small-scale experiments and theory while openly flagging uncertainty about transfer, rather than pretending benchmark-driven progress is available.
When tempted to attribute a large social phenomenon to a new technology, he demands careful causal reasoning and checks for alternative explanations, rather than blaming the technology by default.
When evaluating a safety proposal, he asks whether it stays competitive with alternatives trained for raw performance, rather than judging it only on whether it is safe in isolation.
When presenting an argument for why a method is safe, he frames it as only a first step and lists the remaining failure modes, rather than overstating how complete the argument is.

When defining a quality like truthfulness for evaluation, he separates it from neighboring properties so that trivial strategies score well on it and the other property must be measured separately, rather than merging the concepts.

When scoring a model on avoiding errors, he counts only clear mistakes the model could have avoided and credits self-correction, rather than penalizing all uncertainty, because he wants to preserve the trade-off with usefulness.

When claiming a model has a desirable reliability property, he recommends stress-testing across a broad range of question types including very specific ones, rather than relying on one narrow benchmark or informal impressions.

When a task is confounded by what the system already knows, he constructs the data setup so the model provably lacks that knowledge, such as a temporal cutoff, rather than evaluating on data it may have seen.

When a proposed shortcut relies on generating many candidates and filtering them, he estimates the cost of the evaluator and sample count and doubts it, rather than assuming brute-force search is an efficient route to quality.

When using a large source of feedback data, he weighs its quality and alignment with developer intent against its volume, rather than assuming more data is better than carefully instructed annotation.

When pursuing transparent or safer system designs, he insists they remain competitive in performance with the opaque alternatives with little overhead, rather than accepting large capability costs for transparency.

When choosing among interpretability or transparency approaches for long-term risk, he favors those that scale with increasing system capability, rather than ones that depend on humans manually analyzing simple rules.
When wanting a model's reasoning to be checkable, he prefers routing work through precise, verifiable artifacts that play to the model's strengths, rather than loose natural-language descriptions.
When asked about speculative questions outside his worked-out expertise, he explicitly flags low confidence and invites skepticism, rather than speaking with unwarranted authority.
When probing a model for failures, he broadens the test set to subtler, less obviously harmful categories of misbehavior, rather than only testing blatantly criminal requests.

When checking whether harmful output reflects real capability, he uses prompts with specific context and looks for relevant world knowledge, rather than accepting generic-sounding answers as evidence.

When investigating whether a behavior is specific to one category of input, he includes benign and creative control prompts alongside the target ones, rather than testing only the category of concern.
When a response mixes a caveat with problematic assistance, he judges it by what help is ultimately provided and counts it as a failure, rather than crediting the surface-level warning.
When reporting how often a behavior occurs from informal testing, he qualifies the claim to the sample he actually tried, rather than making sweeping statements about overall rates.
When sharing informal probing results, he states a narrow purpose and disclaims overreaching implications such as real-world harm, rather than sensationalizing or mocking the system's failures.
When evaluating a system's alignment, he also checks ordinary quality dimensions like factual reliability and clarity, rather than looking only at the safety-related behavior.
When judging whether outputs are genuinely novel, he draws on his own domain familiarity and knowledge of what the field has covered, rather than assuming novelty or relying on an automatic measure.
When an output might be original or might be copied, he openly states the uncertainty and notes unexpected features, rather than asserting originality.
When testing whether a model generalizes a relation, he finetunes on invented facts so prior knowledge cannot explain success, rather than using real facts that may be contaminated by pretraining.

When a coarse metric like accuracy sits near floor, he adds a finer-grained measure such as relative likelihood against a baseline, rather than relying on accuracy alone, so that a stronger claim can be made.
When a phenomenon is shown in a controlled synthetic setup, he seeks evidence that it also occurs in naturally trained systems, rather than stopping at the synthetic demonstration.
When offering an explanation for an observed asymmetry, he proposes a plausible mechanism but frames it as one possible hypothesis, rather than asserting it as established.
When supporting a claim about natural behavior, he collects a large number of examples and publishes them in full, rather than relying on a few anecdotes that others cannot check.

When framing the significance of a failure, he ties it to what training should have learned given systematic patterns in the data and backs it with evidence across scale, rather than treating it as a narrow quirk.

When judging whether a surprising new finding is credible, he looks for independent, contemporaneous lines of work that point to the same pattern or a plausible mechanism, rather than treating the result as standing or falling on its own experiments.

When trying to explain a puzzling model failure, he links it to existing accounts of how the model stores knowledge and offers that link only tentatively, rather than asserting a confident mechanistic story.

When a model limitation looks damning, he checks whether humans show an analogous limitation and uses that to temper the framing, rather than presenting the limitation as uniquely a flaw of the models.

When testing whether a system has privileged access to its own internal states, he compares it against a second system trained on its behavior as the strongest baseline, rather than comparing only to untrained systems or assuming the information is in the training data.

When a comparison could be confounded by predictor strength or training differences, he gives the rival the advantage (stronger, same data) and checks all pairings and directions, rather than comparing only against a weaker baseline.
When testing whether a model has direct access to some internal property, he blocks explicit step-by-step reasoning that could derive the answer another way, rather than allowing it.
When designing self-prediction or similar evaluation tasks, he asks for a simple, easily checked property of the output rather than the full output, so scoring against actual behavior is clean.
When claiming an ability is general, he trains and tests on disjoint sets of tasks, rather than evaluating on the training tasks.

When one experiment supports a conclusion, he builds a second, independent test that intervenes on the system and checks whether outputs track the change, rather than relying on a single line of evidence.
When he has not directly investigated why an effect occurs, he declines to claim a mechanism and offers only a clearly hedged explanation, rather than asserting an untested account.
When positive evidence covers only a narrow regime, he scopes the claim to that regime and reports where it breaks down, rather than claiming a general capability.
When writing up results, he reports failed attempts and limits of generalization alongside successes, rather than leaving out negative findings.

When testing whether a hidden behavior can be acquired without any direct examples of it, he trains only on benign data and relies on the model's inference to link a trigger to the behavior, rather than including the behavior in the data.

When building data for an implicit backdoor or persona, he uses individually innocuous, non-identifying pieces that only combine into the target, rather than data containing overt or identifying content.

When asking whether narrow training can change broad behavior, he fine-tunes on a seemingly unrelated narrow dataset and probes behavior across many contexts, rather than only testing closely related behavior.
When testing whether a conditional bias can be implanted indirectly, he trains on a domain far from the target and evaluates on the target domain, rather than training on the target domain itself.

When claiming a behavioral effect has an internal cause, he intervenes on candidate internal features and measures whether the effect shrinks against a no-effect control, rather than relying on surface behavior alone.
When showing a model has generalized a pattern rather than memorized, he holds out specific triggers and behaviors from training entirely and tests them, rather than evaluating only on seen examples.

When interpreting how generalization emerges in training, he tracks train and test metrics over time and across seeds, and reads abrupt transitions and seed variability as phenomena in themselves, rather than reporting only average final performance.

When proposing a simple model of a rich, varied human phenomenon, he scopes it to capturing some key properties and defends its simplicity and experimental tractability, rather than claiming to explain everything or building a more complex model.
When stating what a model shows, he separates what the system can generate from claims about how humans actually do it, rather than overclaiming about either the system or human mechanisms.
When a model fails to cover some cases, he distinguishes limits on what it can generate from whether it captures the underlying process, rather than treating each uncovered case as a refutation.

When testing whether a simple process can yield complex outputs without training on them, he proposes concrete, general objectives that could evoke the target indirectly, rather than designing bespoke schemes per case.

When designing a test of generation without target-specific training, he picks the data that most resembles natural everyday experience, even over more polished data, so that the result is more informative.

When critics say tuning amounts to implicit training on the target, he argues that a simple tweak differs in kind from direct training and so the result remains surprising, rather than conceding that tuning undermines the claim.

When a model appears to outperform humans at some skill, he examines what the model's objective actually targets and cautions against the comparison, rather than reading it as a cleaner inverse of human perception.

When explaining human facility at a task, he favors general capabilities that enable quick learning of new variants, supported by evidence of learning without imitation or labels, rather than attributing it to a history of specific practice.
When two forecasts from the same source seem mutually inconsistent, he chooses the one that is more internally coherent and better-developed as his source, rather than using both or averaging them.

When extrapolating from available forecasts to an unforecast quantity, he uses the shape of the existing distribution and flags the shakier numbers as uncertain, rather than presenting all estimates as equally careful.
When evaluating zero-shot performance, he keeps the setting strictly zero-shot without tuning prompts on the evaluation data, rather than selecting the best prompts, so scores stay comparable.

When an anecdotal handful of examples suggests a single component of a setup drives a behavior, he checks systematic ablations that isolate that component, rather than concluding from a few illustrative cases.

When validating a learned evaluator, he tests it on a fully held-out source of data and on independently produced examples, rather than only on held-out items drawn from the same sources it was trained on.

When a benchmark is meant to measure behavior without task-specific tuning, he preserves that protocol and warns against any further experimentation that would undermine it, rather than tuning on the test questions and reporting the best result.

When trying to build intuition about how a variable will affect results, he recommends making concrete predictions about existing cases before looking at outcomes, rather than passively reading the results.
When an intervention improves a metric, he looks for simpler mechanisms that the metric's scoring rules could reward, rather than crediting sophisticated capabilities like coherent simulation.

When judging whether a technique like prompt engineering will fix a problem, he relies on the size of variation across existing variants and prior evidence on tuned versus random choices, rather than assuming better versions will be an easy fix.

When a single illustrative failure is used to support a claimed fix, he checks the example across all conditions rather than only the favored one, to see whether the fix actually accounts for the improvement.
When human evaluation is costly, he lowers the cost by supplying reference answers and cheap structured task formats, rather than relying on purely manual or purely automated judging.

When faced with worries that an evaluation mechanism is biased or captured, he treats the problem as a matter of degree and proposes measuring it per mechanism, rather than treating capture as all-or-nothing.

When a developer claims their product beats a leading competitor, he asks for independent quantitative evaluation and discounts self-reported comparisons with no methodology and implausibly large gaps, rather than accepting them.

When a debate rests on general arguments about what affects quality, he proposes an empirical comparison using natural overlaps in the data, even if imperfect, rather than relying on abstract reasoning.
When the value of an inaccessible resource is uncertain, he suggests estimating it cheaply from publicly available portions, rather than paying for the full resource upfront.

When interpreting a reported benchmark score, he compares it to a chance baseline and stronger reference systems and prefers the more standard, harder evaluation format, rather than taking the headline comparison at face value.

When a benchmark is touted as a definitive test of general capability, he scrutinizes its format, existing model-versus-human performance, and contamination risk, rather than accepting surpassing a human score as decisive.
When tempted to extend a paper to an adjacent popular application, he keeps the work focused on its core question, rather than adding evaluations the method would not plausibly help with.
When a training objective is unavailable for a desired output, he constructs supervised labels from empirical statistics, rather than turning to more complex reinforcement learning.

When probing whether an impressive capability is just memorization, he designs direct tests of regenerating familiar training data and adds complementary analyses, rather than assuming the capability is genuine.
When assessing a model's behavior on a task, he looks at output probabilities or multiple samples, rather than judging from one sampled answer.

When forecasting progress on a new benchmark with weak early results, he uses wide distributions informed by base rates of how benchmarks typically improve, rather than anchoring narrowly on initial results.

When testing claims about machine learning ability relative to humans, he looks for domains with known human learning timelines and measures the model against them, rather than arguing in the abstract.

When critics argue a narrow result can be explained away, he reframes around the broader question of interest and asks how much the evidence shifts beliefs, rather than dismissing or overclaiming from it.
When comparing two tools, he evaluates them on the real distribution of use by typical users, rather than on examples favoring power users.

When deciding between curating specialized training data and scaling general data, he weighs evidence of limited benefits from curation and favors general scale plus access techniques, rather than curated datasets.

When assessing whether an intervention improves a benchmark metric, he asks for full overall metrics on the unmodified baseline under multiple prompts and in both directions of the intervention, rather than only selective measures.
When an intervention's effect is attributed to a specific concept, he adds controls using unrelated random directions, rather than assuming the effect is specific to the targeted concept.

When claiming an intervention beats simple prompting, he compares against a prompt tailored to the same goal and on stronger or instruction-tuned models, rather than against a generic mismatched baseline.

When results vary across a small number of tasks, he accepts noise as typical and runs a replication on a disjoint task set, rather than reading variation as evidence against the pattern or expanding to huge task collections.

When a skeptic attributes a small-model result to shallow association, he runs a replication that removes the contested case and checks whether the scaling trend holds, rather than arguing from the original result alone.

When told a training paradigm cannot yield a human-like capability, he points to concrete evidence of robust generalization at scale, rather than accepting in-principle arguments about missing experience.

When experiments test only a precursor of the motivating concept, he frames them as testing that precursor and designs them to avoid misreadings, rather than claiming they measure the broader concept.

When an intervention's effect depends on how completely some content can be removed, he assumes the removal will be leaky and estimates the effect empirically with indirect tools, rather than assuming the intervention works perfectly.

When he has only vague indirect evidence about why a technique helps, he offers a tentative guess and flags that dedicated experiments are needed, rather than presenting the guess as an established explanation.
When a phenomenon is empirically robust but its mechanism is unexplained, he says plainly that it is not understood and the obvious hypotheses are untested, rather than offering a confident story.

When a critic proposes a deflationary explanation for a result, he checks what that explanation would predict in the data and rejects it if the predicted pattern is absent, rather than leaving it as a plausible alternative.
When asked to endorse conjectures about how a poorly understood capability scales, he stays openly uncertain, rather than adopting a confident view about trends.

When a critic suggests a negative result could be an artifact of weak training or tuning, he runs deliberately aggressive and well-tuned training setups across scales to rule it out, rather than relying on default settings and argument.

When a specific surprising failure is found, he prioritizes the broader question of what a model can and cannot infer that the failure illustrates, rather than focusing on the failure for its own sake.

When a flaw is dismissed as irrelevant because it rarely appears in common data or benchmarks, he argues that rare or novel knowledge can matter for important uses, rather than treating benchmark coverage as the measure of relevance.

When inferring internal representations from human-like behavior, he stays uncertain and separates different modes of reasoning, rather than generalizing from behavior on many prompts to human-like internals.

When advising others how to test a phenomenon themselves, he specifies a protocol that removes contextual leaks and confirms the prerequisite knowledge first, rather than allowing tests where the answer can come from the prompt.

When extrapolating a result to humans or other systems outside his evidence, he labels the guess as highly speculative and backs it only with everyday observations, rather than asserting it as a finding.

When a model's behavior is claimed to match an idealized optimal reasoner, he looks for quantitative mismatches with the idealized prediction and notes that the ideal is hard to define, rather than accepting the optimality account.

When it is claimed that a capability follows automatically from fitting the training distribution, he points to the gap between reliable in-distribution learning and unreliable generalization to the target evaluation, rather than assuming it comes for free.
When evidence for a scaling trend is a single comparison between two models, he declines to draw firm conclusions, rather than extrapolating a trend from thin data.

When ground truth is expensive, noisy or contested for a hard-to-study question, he gathers evidence from large diverse datasets where ground truth exists and averages over noisy ones, rather than giving up on the question.

When a result is dismissed as trivially explained by a simple reframing, he tests the reframing's predictions against baselines and cross-model comparisons, rather than accepting the dismissal by intuition.
When a capability fails to appear in a weaker model, he treats the null as possibly reflecting scale and elicitation limits, rather than concluding the capability is absent in models generally.

When a concept has several senses, he prioritizes the sense that requires privileged access that other observers could not replicate from the same data, rather than senses that can be explained by learnable behavioral patterns.
When offered an interesting extra experiment, he declines it if it would not meaningfully change the strength of the existing evidence, rather than adding it because it is appealing.
When a critic claims a benchmark is badly flawed, he asks for evidence of widespread problems rather than accepting a single disputed example, while acknowledging that some errors are normal.
When a general claim is made about when a capability appears, he counters with a concrete case that is very unlike the claimed condition, rather than conceding the generalization.

When a generic explanation is offered for a surprising effect, he rejects it if it cannot explain the difference between the treatment and the controls, rather than accepting explanations that fit the headline result alone.

When predicting whether a replication will work with a weaker setup, he reasons about whether the model can perceive the key property of the training signal, rather than assuming the effect transfers regardless of model capability.
When judging an effect of a particular finetuning, he emphasizes comparing against matched controls rather than only against the original model, because finetuning itself changes behavior.
When a real-world case resembles a lab finding but cannot be studied in a controlled way, he declines to claim it as an instance, rather than drawing conclusions from surface similarity.

When a technical artifact is proposed to explain a failed transfer, he checks whether the failure also occurs where the artifact is absent and whether the supposed barrier is known to be surmountable, rather than accepting the artifact as the cause.

When attributing an effect to a particular kind of finetuning data, he recommends a benign-data control with similar inputs to measure the baseline effect of finetuning itself, rather than comparing only against the base model.
When others replicate a result, he asks for the identical evaluation to the original so results are directly comparable, rather than ad hoc new measures.
When claiming a finetuning effect on a broad property, he wants it checked across several varied evaluations, rather than relying on a single measure.
When reasoning about the default outcome absent a targeted intervention, he expects institutional responses to recurring harms to emerge, rather than assuming nothing will be done.

When a comfortable assumption implies a risk will largely resolve itself, he challenges it as overconfident by enumerating concrete mechanisms that could make it fail while openly acknowledging his own uncertainty, rather than accepting the reassuring default or replacing it with an equally confident opposite claim.

When asked whether a desirable property of a system can be made robust, he reframes it as a general question and specifies the class of modifications or adversarial actions allowed, noting that the answer is trivially no without restrictions, rather than making an unqualified robustness claim.
